classification.difficultyReason: Construct a square accurately, verify its diagonal angles and explain its circumcircle using diagonal properties.

content.prompt: Draw a square using the following steps.

children.label: a
children.prompt: First, draw a horizontal line. Construct a vertical line meeting the horizontal line at $D$. With centre $D$ and radius $5$ cm, draw a circle meeting the vertical line at $A$ and the horizontal line at $C$. With centres $A$ and $C$, draw arcs of radius $5$ cm meeting at $B$, their intersection other than $D$. Join $AB$ and $BC$. Explain why $ABCD$ is a square.

answer.short: $AB=BC=CD=DA=5\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ADC=90^\circ$, so $ABCD$ is a square.
answer.worked: $AD=DC=5\text{ cm}$ because they are radii of the circle centred at $D$. Also, $AB=CB=5\text{ cm}$ because the arcs centred at $A$ and $C$ have radius $5\text{ cm}$. Thus all four sides are equal, so $ABCD$ is a rhombus. The horizontal and vertical lines give $\angle ADC=90^\circ$. A rhombus is a parallelogram; its opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary, so all four angles are right angles. Hence $ABCD$ is a square.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Draw the two diagonals, and label their intersection $M$.

answer.worked: Join $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $D$ on the construction from part a. Label their intersection $M$. The diagonals bisect each other, so $AM=MC$ and $BM=MD$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use your protractor to check that the diagonals intersect at right angles, and that they each meet the sides at $45^\circ$.

answer.short: The diagonals intersect at $90^\circ$ and each meets the sides at $45^\circ$.
answer.worked: Measurements on the construction give $90^\circ$ between the diagonals and $45^\circ$ between each diagonal and each adjoining side. A square is a rhombus, so its diagonals meet at right angles and bisect its vertex angles. Each vertex angle is $90^\circ$, so each half is $45^\circ$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Construct the circle with centre $M$ passing through $A$. Notice that it goes through $B$, $C$ and $D$. What property of a square tells us that it must pass through $B$, $C$ and $D$?

answer.short: The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so $MA=MB=MC=MD$.
answer.worked:
Using the same construction, set the compass radius to $MA$ and draw the circle centred at $M$. The diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other. Therefore,
$$MA=MC=\frac{AC}{2},\qquad MB=MD=\frac{BD}{2}.$$
Since $AC=BD$, all four distances from $M$ are equal. Hence the circle through $A$ also passes through $B$, $C$ and $D$.

spec.description: Completed shared construction: square with A above D, C to the right of D, B at the other intersection of the radius-5 cm arcs, both diagonals, their intersection M and the circumcircle. Dashed thin lines distinguish retained compass construction and diagonals from the square and circumcircle.
spec.mathematics: AD=DC=AB=BC=5 cm; angle ADC=90 degrees; M is the common diagonal midpoint; MA=MB=MC=MD. The initial circle is centred at D with radius 5 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only; students construct the entire figure.
